newsitem.title: UK: Bulgaria's future looks bleak despite assurances.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's future looks bleak despite assurances.

text.p: Bulgaria's latest pledges to sort out its sinking currency and meet debt repayments are not enough to instil confidence in foreign investors that the government is serious about economic reform, analysts said on Wednesday.

"We've heard a lot of promises but there are no visible results...The political and economic situation is going to deteriorate over the next three months," said ING Barings East Europe analyst Parvoleta Shtereva.
Key to its chances of a recovery is agreement with the International Monetary Fund for a loan in return for reforms which the government has so far been reluctant to implement.

Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov promised to meet foreign debt repayments later this month of $135 million and set up a new system for the Bulgarian currency, the lev, which has lost more than a third of its value this year.
His comments briefly pushed U.S. Treasury-backed Bulgarian Brady bond prices higher but traders said most investors were very wary of the paper even with its high yield.
A currency board system, demanded by the IMF, would mean that the central bank could print only new lev which it could cover with hard currency.
At the moment it has about $500 million in currency reserves and a similar amount in gold, mostly held within the country, which would be politically difficult to sell off.

Chase Manhattan analyst Robin Hubbard noted that the country's total foreign debt bill this quarter alone was $300 million. "The key issue is whether they receive external finance. If they don't, sooner or later they will run out of money," he said.
Hubbard said the chances of an agreement with the IMF, which would be the trigger for other sources of money from abroad, were only 60:40.
One of the most crucial elements will be signs of government commitment to privatisation which it has dragged its heels on.

Even with the already delayed currency board in place, analysts said Bulgaria's credibility is so poor, having missed so many opportunities for reform in 1996, that it was far from certain the government would have the stamina to maintain the system.

"One of the problems with Bulgaria is that no one stands up and says they will sort out the problems...they are all passing the poison chalice to someone else," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell local currency analyst David Atkinson.
But his bank, while recommending investors stay underweight in Bulgarian debt, was more hopeful in the longer term that the problems would be sorted out.

Confidence in the country has been further damaged by the resignation last month of prime minister Zhan Videnov and signs of further social unrest, with more opposition demonstrations planned this week.
"Social pressures are building up. It won't come to bloodshed but it is something to be watched," Shtereva said.
